governance_classification: RESEARCH DEMONSTRATION PROTOTYPE — NOT FOR LIFE-SAFETY USE

taxonomy_architecture.reconciliation_summary: 19 primary categories (1 Scream, 17 Negative, 1 Ambiguous). When primary is SCREAM, 1 of 6 mutually exclusive subcategories is assigned, yielding exactly 24 canonical leaf classes.

primary_categories.description: Human vocalization with maximal vocal fold excursion, non-linear chaos/subharmonics, and auditory roughness.
Distress, hunger, or pain cry from an infant or toddler (<2 years). Cyclic melody glide, periodic breath bursts.
Adult weeping, sobbing, or tearful vocalizations. Breathy trembling voice without high-frequency chaos.
High-effort projected linguistic speech where lexical words/formants (F1, F2) are intelligible.
Dramatic acting, stage shouts, or radio voice performance without physiological panic dynamics.
High-energy positive celebratory vocalizations from individuals or groups.
Rhythmic unison shouting or chanting from stadium or festival crowds.
Musical sustained vocalization adhering to musical scale pitches, high HNR, vibrato.
Paroxysmal interrupted exhalations during mirth, 4-6 Hz burst cadence.
Sudden inspiratory airflow intake, startle intake, duration < 0.5s, unvoiced turbulence.
High-frequency narrow-band tonal whistle (sports referee, pea whistle, whistling).
Emergency vehicle or electronic siren with periodic sweeping FM tones (500-1800 Hz).
Animal sounds (dogs barking, birds screeching, cats howling).
Industrial buzzers, fire alarms, security beeps.
Fairground machinery, metal squeals, brake friction, pneumatic release.
Amplified musical instruments, heavy bass, drums, synthesizer audio.
Outdoor festival crowd murmur, wind, rain, foot traffic, broad ambience.
Any acoustic event that is clearly non-scream and not covered by other negative classes.
Vocalizations exhibiting severe borderline characteristics or extreme distortion where reliable distinction cannot be made.

scream_subcategories.description: Maximal-effort adult panic/distress scream with extreme broadband chaos.
Suppressed, low-effort, or distant adult distress vocalization.
Prepubescent child scream with high pitch, wide harmonics, lower roughness due to low vocal fold mass.
Abrupt brief startle or shock shriek lasting < 1.0 second.
Continuous prolonged distress phonation exceeding 1.2 seconds.
Scream vocalization embedded in heavy outdoor or crowd noise.
